objectives: Explain who Ahmed Yesevî was.
Explain the words pîr, order and hikmet.
Say what his poems and the Yesevî Path aimed to do.
Use known as, means and aimed to.
content.pedagogy: The opening chapter is full of definitions. A definition chart (word → meaning → example) helps learners handle pîr, order and hikmet, and shows how writers explain words inside a text.
anticipatedMisconceptions: ‘Order’ here means a spiritual path, not a command.
He wrote and recited his poems in plain Turkish, not in Persian.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: known as (extra information) · means · be called · aimed to + verb
Notice (Activity 1): Ahmed Yesevî, known as Pîr-i Turkistan, …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *known like · *the word mean · *aimed spreading.
Use (Activity 4): a person with a title.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: ah-MED ye-se-VÎ, PÎR-i tur-kis-TAN, hik-MET.
Stress: re-CITE, SPIR-it-u-al, FOUND-er.
beforeReading: Ask: “Do you know anyone who is called by a special title?”
duringReading: First reading: Who was Ahmed Yesevî?
Second reading: complete the definition chart for pîr, order and hikmet.
Find what his poems aimed to do.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Definition chart; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: a person with a title; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why is Yesevî called Pîr-i Turkistan?
Why was it important to write in plain Turkish?
What is the difference between a poet and a spiritual guide?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Pîr-i Turkistan” and “Hikmet” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: recite, plain, Persian language, Sufi master, spiritual guide, wisdom, spread, founder.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the definition chart with the three words written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short dictionary entry for pîr, order and hikmet.

formativeAssessment: Uses known as or means correctly.
expectedResponses: Ahmed Yesevî, known as Pîr-i Turkistan, was the first great Sufi poet to write in plain Turkish. ‘Pîr’ means a Sufi master or spiritual guide, and his poems are called ‘hikmet’.
content.transferTask: Write about a person known by a title.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners explain the key words in their own words?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “known as” and one with “means”.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain in three sentences who Ahmed Yesevî was and why he is important. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads up to “Turkish-Islamic culture” and B reads the rest. Each explains the main idea and one detail. The partner asks one follow-up question.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the sentence about the word “pîr”. Asker asks “What does ‘pîr’ mean?” Checker checks the three meanings in the text.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A visitor at a book fair asks, “Why is Ahmed Yesevî called Pîr-i Turkistan?” The learner explains in two or three sentences.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “His poems are called ‘hikmet’ (wisdom).” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, who Ahmed Yesevî was and what his poems are called. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The writer explains two words in brackets. Which words, and why?” (Order and hikmet, because readers may not know their special meaning here.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners explain “pîr”, “order” and “hikmet” in their own words.

thinkAloud.sentence: He was also the founder of the Yesevî Order (here, ‘order’ means a spiritual path).
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: I know “order” as a command. The brackets tell me that here it has a different meaning: a spiritual path. A good reader checks brackets for help. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “In the Persian language, the word ‘pîr’ means a Sufi master, spiritual guide, or elder.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What does “pîr” mean in Persian?

onlineTask.post: Write two or three sentences: Which poet from your culture writes in plain language?
onlineTask.reply: Ask your classmate one question about his or her poet.

objectives: Describe Yesevî’s childhood and education.
Explain the old and modern names of Yesi.
Explain what Turkestan was like in his time.
Use It is believed that and which is now.
content.pedagogy: A short biography chapter with historical uncertainty and modern place names. A then-and-now chart (old name → modern name) helps learners link history with today’s map.
anticipatedMisconceptions: He was born in Sayram and moved to Yesi; he was not born in Yesi.
The Karakhanid dates (840–1212) are the dates of the state, not of Yesevî’s life.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: It is believed that · which is now · grow up · at a time when
Notice (Activity 1): It is believed that he was born …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then correct errors.
Likely errors: *It believed that · *various field.
Use (Activity 4): a place then and now.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: SAY-ram, YE-si, ka-ra-KHA-nids, AR-slan BA-ba.
Stress: ed-u-CA-tion, VAR-i-ous.
beforeReading: Ask: “Do you know a city that had another name in the past?”
duringReading: First reading: Where did Yesevî grow up?
Second reading: complete the then-and-now chart.
Find what Turkestan was like.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–10 First reading; 10–16 Then-and-now chart; 16–20 Quick Challenge; 20–34 Language Focus 1–3; 34–42 Use: a place then and now; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why does the writer say “It is believed that”?
Why was Turkestan a good place to study?
Who was his first teacher?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Sayram” and “The Karakhanids” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: received, grew up, various, fields, era.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with the old names written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short timeline of Yesevî’s early life.

formativeAssessment: Gives the modern name of Yesi.
Uses It is believed that correctly.
expectedResponses: It is believed that Yesevî was born in Sayram. He moved to Yesi, which is now the city of Turkestan in Kazakhstan, and studied with Arslan Baba.
content.transferTask: Write about a place that had another name in the past.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners separate facts from beliefs?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “It is believed that” about Yesevî.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners describe Ahmed Yesevî’s childhood and education in three steps. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner explains to a partner where Yesi is today. The partner restates it with “which is now”.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the last sentence. Listener notes what Turkestan was at that time. Writer writes it in one short sentence.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A traveler in Kazakhstan asks, “Why is the city of Turkestan famous?” The learner answers using the chapter.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “There, he studied with Arslan Baba and received a good education.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, where Ahmed Yesevî was born and where he studied as a child. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Why does the chapter start with ‘It is believed that’?” (Historians are not completely sure about his birth.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners name Sayram, Yesi and Arslan Baba, and they use “It is believed that” correctly.

thinkAloud.sentence: It is believed that he was born in the town of Sayram, in East Turkestan, during the second half of the 11th century.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “It is believed that” tells me this is what people think, not a fact everyone has proven. So I should say “probably” when I retell it. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “Ahmed Yesevî moved to the city of Yesi in Turkestan (which is now the city of Turkestan in Kazakhstan) at a young age.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What is the city of Yesi called today?

onlineTask.post: Write two or three sentences: Where did you go to school first, and what do you remember?
onlineTask.reply: Ask your classmate one question about his or her first school.

content.chapter: Chapter 3: Master and Return to Yesi
objectives: Describe Yesevî’s years in Bukhara in order.
Explain the role of Sheikh Yûsuf el-Hemedânî.
Explain what Yesevî did after his master died.
Use who clauses, after, when and then.
content.pedagogy: A chain of teachers and students: Arslan Baba, Hemedânî, Yesevî and Gucdüvânî. A simple chain diagram helps learners keep the names and see how knowledge passed from person to person.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Yesevî handed over his duty to Gucdüvânî; Gucdüvânî was not his teacher.
He returned to Yesi at the end and died there in 1166.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: who (defining) · after / when + past · then · hand over
Notice (Activity 1): a famous Sufi master who played the greatest role …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the time words, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *a master which · *After died Arslan Baba.
Use (Activity 4): a teacher who trained me.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: bu-KHA-ra, YÛ-suf el-he-me-DÂ-nî, ab-dül-HÂ-lik guc-dü-VÂ-nî.
Stress: SCHOL-ar, GUID-ance.
duringReading: First reading: Who trained Yesevî in Bukhara?
Second reading: draw the chain of teachers and students.
Find what he did at the end of his life.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Chain diagram; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: a teacher who trained me; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did Yesevî go to Bukhara?
Why was Hemedânî important for him?
Why did he hand over his duty before he returned?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Bukhara” and “Sheikh Yûsuf el-Hemedânî” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: scholar, training, handed over, guidance.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chain diagram with the names written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write the story of the four teachers and students in six sentences.

expectedResponses: After Arslan Baba died, Yesevî went to Bukhara and studied with Sheikh Yûsuf el-Hemedânî, who played the greatest role in training him. Later, he handed over his duty and returned to Yesi.
content.transferTask: Write about a person who trained you.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners follow the chain of teachers?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “after” and one with “who” about Yesevî.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain what happened in Bukhara and why Ahmed Yesevî went back to Yesi. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads paragraph 1 and B reads paragraph 2. Each explains the main event of his or her paragraph. Together they make a short time line.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the sentence about Sheikh Yûsuf el-Hemedânî. Asker asks “What role did he play?” Checker finds “the greatest role”.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A student asks, “Who was the most important teacher of Ahmed Yesevî?” The learner answers and gives one reason.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “He then returned to Yesi and continued his spiritual guidance there until he died in 1166.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, who taught Ahmed Yesevî in Bukhara and what he did after his master died. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Why did Ahmed Yesevî hand over his duty before he returned to Yesi?” (Someone had to continue the work in Bukhara.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners name both sheikhs and use “after” and “then” in the right order.

thinkAloud.sentence: Later, he handed over his duty as a spiritual leader to Sheikh Abdülhâlik Gucdüvânî.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “Later” tells me this happened after his master died. I put it on my time line before his return to Yesi. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “After Arslan Baba died, Ahmed Yesevî went to Bukhara.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: Why was Bukhara important at that time?

onlineTask.post: Write two or three sentences about a teacher who played a big role in your life.
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate with one question.

objectives: Say where Yesevî became widely known.
Explain why people loved him.
Describe the nomadic communities near the Syr Darya River.
Use because and because of.
content.pedagogy: A very short chapter with one key reason. The contrast between “because” and “because of” is clear in the text, so it is a good moment to focus on it.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Nomadic communities moved from place to place; they did not live in one city.
People loved him for his language and wisdom, not for power.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: because of + noun phrase · because + clause · so
Notice (Activity 1): because of his simple language …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *because of he used · *because his simple language.
Use (Activity 4): a speaker people love.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: tash-KENT, SYR DAR-ya.
Stress: no-MAD-ic, com-MU-ni-ties.
beforeReading: Ask: “What makes a speaker easy to understand?”
duringReading: First reading: Where did Yesevî become widely known?
Second reading: underline the reason.
Find the river.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–9 First reading; 9–14 Reasons; 14–18 Quick Challenge; 18–33 Language Focus 1–3; 33–42 Use: a speaker people love; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did simple language matter to nomadic people?
How can words win the love of people?
What is the difference between knowledge and wisdom?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Nomadic Communities” and “The Syr Darya River” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: widely, communities.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the frames: because of his … / because he …
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short dialogue between two nomads who have just heard Yesevî.

expectedResponses: Yesevî became widely known among the nomadic Turkic communities near Tashkent and along the Syr Darya River. People loved him because of his simple language and his words of wisdom.
content.transferTask: Write about a person whose words people love.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners use because and because of correctly?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “because of” and one with “because”.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain why the nomadic Turkic communities loved Ahmed Yesevî. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: One learner explains the chapter to a partner who has not read it. The partner restates it with “because of”.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the second sentence. Asker asks “What two things won the love of the people?” Checker checks both.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A teacher asks, “How can we make difficult ideas easy for children?” The learner answers using Ahmed Yesevî as an example.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “He won the love of the people because of his simple language and his words of wisdom (hikmet).” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, why nomadic Turkic people loved Ahmed Yesevî. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Why might simple language be important for nomadic communities?” (Many people could not read, so they needed words that were easy to remember.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners use “because of” with a noun and name the Syr Darya River or Tashkent.

thinkAloud.sentence: He won the love of the people because of his simple language and his words of wisdom (hikmet).
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: After “because of” I find nouns, not a full sentence. These two nouns are the reasons. “Because” would need a subject and a verb. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “During this period, he became widely known among the nomadic Turkic communities that lived near Tashkent and along the Syr Darya River.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: Where did these communities live?

onlineTask.post: Write two or three sentences: Why do people remember simple poems and songs easily?

content.chapter: Chapter 5: The Yesevî Path and the Mausoleum
objectives: Explain how the Yesevî Path spread.
Describe the history of the mausoleum from Timur to TİKA.
Explain why people wanted to be buried near it.
Use the past passive and the present perfect passive.
content.pedagogy: A long chapter with dates and a building story. A timeline (1166 → 1389–1405 → 1405 → 2003 → today) organizes the facts, and the passive appears naturally because the building is the topic.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Timur ordered the mausoleum, but it was left unfinished when he died.
TİKA completed the restoration and landscaping; it did not build the mausoleum.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: was + past participle · have been + past participle · order something to be built · to be buried
Notice (Activity 1): the construction was left unfinished.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then correct errors.
Likely errors: *is still respect · *have been complete.
Use (Activity 4): a historic building I know.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: TI-mur, ka-ZAKHS, KIR-giz, UZ-beks, TURK-men, TÎ-ka.
Stress: mau-so-LE-um, HER-i-tage, res-to-RA-tion.
beforeReading: Ask: “Which historic building in your country has been restored?”
duringReading: First reading: Who ordered the mausoleum?
Second reading: complete the timeline.
Find why people wanted to be buried near it.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Timeline; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: a historic building; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did Timur visit the tomb?
What does the burial tradition show?
Why is the mausoleum a shared heritage?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “The Mausoleum” and “UNESCO 2003” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: respected, spread across, tomb, steppes, to be buried, Heritage, landscaping, grave, complex, construction.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the timeline with the dates written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short visitor guide for the mausoleum with three passive sentences.

expectedResponses: Timur ordered a mausoleum to be built over Yesevî’s grave, but it was left unfinished in 1405. In 2003, it was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List, and its restoration has been completed by TİKA.
content.transferTask: Write about a historic building you know.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners use the timeline to order the facts?

exitTicket: Write one passive sentence about the mausoleum.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain why the mausoleum of Ahmed Yesevî is important. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads paragraph 1 and B reads paragraph 2. Each explains the main idea and one date. The partner asks a follow-up question.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the sentences about the burial tradition. Asker asks “Why did people buy land near the mausoleum?” Checker finds “For this reason”.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A tour guide at the mausoleum in Turkestan welcomes visitors and gives a one-minute introduction.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “This mausoleum and complex represent a shared cultural heritage of the Turkic-Islamic world.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, who built the mausoleum of Ahmed Yesevî and why it is still important. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “What does the burial tradition show about Ahmed Yesevî?” (His deep influence on the people of the steppes.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners give the dates 1405 and 2003 correctly and name Timur and TİKA.

thinkAloud.sentence: This tradition clearly shows the deep influence of Ahmed Yesevî.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “This tradition” points back to the sentence before: people bought land to be buried near the mausoleum. The writer uses it as evidence of his influence. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “However, the construction was left unfinished when Timur died in 1405.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: Why was the construction left unfinished?

onlineTask.post: Write two or three sentences about a historic building in your town.
onlineTask.reply: Reply to a classmate with one question about his or her building.

objectives: Explain why Yesevî chose Turkish.
Describe his education and his goals.
Explain how his teachings spread.
Use However, which (whole idea) and Thanks to.
content.pedagogy: The chapter explains a language choice and its effect on identity. A three-column chart (Arabic / Persian / Turkish) shows the roles of the languages, and learners connect the choice of language with the aim of reaching ordinary people.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Yesevî knew the scholarly languages well; he chose Turkish on purpose.
He sent the scholars he trained to the Turkmen tribes; he did not travel to all of them himself.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: which (referring to a whole idea) · However · Thanks to + noun · in a way that
Notice (Activity 1): …, which helped develop a Turkish identity.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the linkers, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *Thanks to his followers spread · *However he chose (no comma).
Use (Activity 4): why my language matters.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: ha-NA-fi, MAD-ra-sa, sha-REE-a, dî-VÂN-ı hik-MET.
Stress: i-DEN-ti-ty, LIT-er-a-ture, in-tro-DUCE.
beforeReading: Ask: “Which languages do you use at home, at school and online?”
duringReading: First reading: Why did Yesevî choose Turkish?
Second reading: complete the three-language chart.
Find his main goal.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–17 Language chart; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: why my language matters; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why was it unusual to write religious poems in Turkish?
How can a language help build an identity?
Why did he use simple and clear teachings?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Arabic and Persian” and “Dîvân-ı Hikmet” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: strict, introduce, the universe, identity, principles.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with one example in each column.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short speech by Yesevî explaining why he writes in Turkish.

formativeAssessment: Uses However or Thanks to correctly.
expectedResponses: People used Arabic for religion and Persian for literature. However, Yesevî wrote in Turkish, which helped develop a Turkish identity. Thanks to his followers, his path spread to many places.
content.transferTask: Write about why your language matters to you.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners connect the language choice with identity?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “However” and one with “Thanks to”.

rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the middle of the first paragraph.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain why Ahmed Yesevî chose Turkish and what he wanted to teach. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: A learner explains to a partner which language people used for what. The partner restates it with “However”.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the sentence about scholars and tribes. Asker asks “What did the scholars teach the tribes?” Checker checks the answer.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A classmate asks, “Why is it important to learn about religion in your own language?” The learner answers using the chapter.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “However, Yesevî chose to write his poems in Turkish, which helped develop a Turkish identity in Islamic culture.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, why Ahmed Yesevî wrote in Turkish and what he wanted to teach the Turks. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Why does the writer first say which languages people used?” (To show that choosing Turkish was unusual and important.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners name the language for education, the language for literature and Yesevî’s choice.

thinkAloud.sentence: However, Yesevî chose to write his poems in Turkish, which helped develop a Turkish identity in Islamic culture.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “However” tells me Yesevî did something different from others. The “which” part tells me the result of his choice. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “His main goal was to spread Islam among the Turks.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What was his main goal?

onlineTask.post: Write two or three sentences: Why is it important to read poems in your home language?

content.chapter: Chapter 7: The Path of Wisdom and Society
objectives: Explain the main goal of wisdom for Yesevî.
List the bad feelings and good values in the chapter.
Describe the social problems in his poems.
Use must, not only … but also and even if.
content.pedagogy: The chapter moves from inner life (ego, greed, patience) to society (orphans, strangers, cruel rulers). A two-part chart (inner life / society) helps learners see that, for Yesevî, wisdom is about both.
anticipatedMisconceptions: “True wisdom means being a good and real human being” is a summary of his view, not a religious rule.
He criticized dishonest judges and cruel rulers, not all judges and rulers.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: must + base verb · not only … but also · even if · those who
Notice (Activity 1): did not only focus on … but also wrote …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then correct errors.
Likely errors: *must to develop · *Education and self-discipline is.
Use (Activity 4): being a good person today.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: hu-MIL-i-ty, PA-tience, OR-phans, op-PRESSED.
Linking: “not only” /nɒt ˈoʊnli/.
beforeReading: Ask: “What makes a person truly good?”
duringReading: First reading: What is the main goal of wisdom?
Second reading: complete the chart: inner life / society.
Find whom he criticized.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Chart; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: being a good person; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What does it mean to leave the ego behind?
Why does Yesevî say religion is not just about sin and reward?
Which social problems from his poems still exist today?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Good Values” and “Social Problems” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: behind, sin, reward, religious, greed, patience, humility, dishonest.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with “greed” and “orphans” written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short poem of four lines with Yesevî’s advice in modern English.

formativeAssessment: Uses not only … but also correctly.
expectedResponses: For Yesevî, the main goal of wisdom is to leave the ego behind. He not only wrote about religious topics but also about social problems, such as caring for orphans and strangers.
content.transferTask: Write about what a good person must do today.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners connect inner values with social action?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “not only … but also”.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain Ahmed Yesevî’s idea of wisdom and two social problems he wrote about. The partner checks one fact in the book.

objectives: Explain the two ways the Qur’an looks at wisdom.

anticipatedMisconceptions: “While” here compares; it does not mean “at the same time”.
“To prevent” is the original meaning of the Arabic word; wisdom prevents ignorance and injustice.

Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.

Use (Activity 4): the wisdom behind a rule.

content.transferTask: Write about the wisdom behind a rule.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners explain the difference between rules and wisdom?

“It does not matter who says them” means that useful knowledge is valuable whoever says it.

metadata.title: Ahmed Yesevî B1 — Teacher’s Book

metadata.targetLearners: Learners who can follow connected texts about history, ideas and values, and who can produce supported explanations and short reflections.
metadata.purpose: Develop evidence-based B1 reading, listening, speaking and writing through Ahmed Yesevî: his life and teachers, the Yesevî Path and the mausoleum, his choice of Turkish, his ideas about wisdom and teaching, the Dîvân-ı Hikmet and its lines, using the Language Focus attached to every story chapter.
metadata.approachDesc: Every story chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading establish meaning and evidence; the Quick Challenge checks comprehension. Grammar is then learned inductively: in the Language Focus, learners first NOTICE a form in a real chapter sentence and work out what it does, then BUILD it in controlled, meaningful practice, and finally USE it in connected YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own world.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 13 Quick Challenges, text-evidence checks, chapter Language Focus tasks (Notice → Build → Use), exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review and Final Challenge.

formative: Short spoken and written Use tasks

readingFramework.before: Activate only what the chapter needs: a short question, a map, a date or a picture.
readingFramework.during: Listen first for gist (when the audio is ready), then read and follow the chapter’s own structure: definitions, a timeline, a building story, ideas with reasons, quotations with sources or poem lines.
readingFramework.after: Complete the Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (notice → build → use), then a connected B1 transfer about the learners’ own world.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Word Notes are the bold words of the teacher-approved text. Prioritize them and the words needed for the chapter’s key idea.
vocabularyApproach.method: Infer meaning from context or a picture before any direct explanation.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse vocabulary in Language Focus tasks, exit tickets and the Language Review.

metadata.grammarApproach: Inductive and text-based. Start from the story sentence, ask a meaning question (What does this form tell us?), let learners formulate the rule in their own words, then confirm it and practice it in context. Rule explanations appear in the app only after learners answer.
grammarSequence: Ch1: known as (extra information) · means · be called · aimed to + verb
Ch2: It is believed that · which is now · grow up · at a time when
Ch3: who (defining) · after / when + past · then · hand over
Ch4: because of + noun phrase · because + clause · so
Ch5: was + past participle · have been + past participle · order something to be built · to be buried
Ch6: which (referring to a whole idea) · However · Thanks to + noun · in a way that
Ch7: must + base verb · not only … but also · even if · those who
Ch8: only possible if · even if · so that · For this reason
Ch9: be believed to + verb · passive with by · himself (emphasis) · probably · pass down
Ch10: While (contrast) · Without + noun · so that · come from
Ch11: so … either · In fact · It does not matter who / where · invite someone to + verb
Ch12: who (defining) · turn … into · still · be like + noun
Ch13: It would be better for … to + verb · if (first conditional) · even if · having + past participle

languageFocus: Every one of the 13 chapters has a Language Focus set built as Notice → Build → Use (4 activities).
Use the Language Focus after basic comprehension and the Quick Challenge.
Always start from the story sentence and ask a meaning question before naming the form.
The Use step is connected spoken or written production about a new, non-story situation.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Reduce linguistic load without lowering the thinking target: one paragraph at a time, charts given in part, picture cards, audio replay, sentence frames and oral rehearsal. Extend by asking for one more sentence or one more reason from the book, not by introducing outside facts.

sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful teaching
notes: Keep explanations within the wording of the book; do not add outside details or opinions.

Chapter 11 quotes verses of the Qur’an and a hadith with their sources; Chapter 13 gives lines from the Dîvân that mention verses and the sayings of the Prophet. These belong to the teacher-approved text; they are read as they are, without extra comment, and the exercises do not change their words.
Chapter 10 explains religious ideas such as haram, helal and Maqasid al-Sharia in the words of the book; keep the discussion within these words.
Chapter 9 says that the works are “believed to belong” to Yesevî and were “probably” written down later; present these as the writer’s careful explanations.
Bracketed Turkish words and the Turkish poem lines belong to the teacher-approved story; they are read as they are.

globalCitizenship.title: Global Citizenship and Cultural Bridges
globalCitizenship.description: Ahmed Yesevî and Hakîm Ata link Central Asia with questions every community faces today: how to teach with simple words, how to do a duty with care and how to welcome guests.

themes.title: Language and identity:
themes.description: Yesevî chose Turkish so that ordinary people could understand (Chapter 6). Discuss how languages help people keep their identity today.

themes.title: Shared heritage:
themes.description: The mausoleum is on the UNESCO World Heritage List and is shared by the Turkic-Islamic world (Chapter 5). Discuss how countries protect shared heritage.

themes.title: Caring for others:
themes.description: Yesevî wrote about orphans, strangers and oppressed people (Chapter 7). Discuss who needs care in communities today.

themes.title: Learning with love:
themes.description: Yesevî’s education method was centered on love (Chapter 8). Discuss what makes learning joyful in schools around the world.

valuesEducation.title: TYMM Values in Action
valuesEducation.description: Use only values the chapter really shows. Ask for the sentence first, then connect the value to a small action learners can do and see. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/erdem-deger-eylem-cercevesi.

items.label: D14 Respect
items.value: Respect: Turkic peoples still respect Yesevî, and he asked people not to hurt anyone, even non-believers (Chapters 5, 7 and 13).

items.label: D20 Helpfulness
items.value: Helpfulness: Yesevî wrote about caring for orphans and strangers and helping oppressed people (Chapter 7).

items.label: D16 Responsibility

items.label: D3 Diligence
items.value: Diligence: Yesevî studied with great teachers in Yesi and Bukhara, and education and self-discipline are very important on the path of wisdom (Chapters 3 and 7).

test.title: End-of-Level Test B1
test.when: Give the test when the class has finished the B1 books it reads this term. It has four parts and takes about 70 minutes plus a short speaking test for each learner.
parts: Reading and Language (45 minutes): in the app. The learner gets a test code at the end.
Writing (25 minutes): on paper. Write an article for your school website about a person you admire. (100–130 words)
Speaking (about 8 minutes): one learner with the teacher, in 2 parts.
Scoring: type the test code in “Score a test”, then score Writing and Speaking with the bands. Copy the pilot line for the pilot results sheet.

metadata.title: Ahmed Yesevî B1 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Read • Find • Check • Build • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 25 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: B1 learners who study Ahmed Yesevî alone or with a teacher.
learningGoals: Understand the 13 chapters of Ahmed Yesevî.
Find evidence in the text before answering.
Follow the life, teachers and heritage of Ahmed Yesevî.
Explain his ideas about language, wisdom and teaching with evidence from the book.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in connected sentences.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Read (and listen, when the audio is ready) before the Quick Challenge.
Repair wrong answers with the text.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 13.

readingDiary.intro: Keep this diary when you finish the book. Write short answers.
prompts: The date I finished the book:
My favorite chapter, and one reason:
One idea of Ahmed Yesevî that I would like to remember:
One sentence for a friend: “Read this book because …”
One new word I want to keep:
The next book I want to read in the library:

sections.title: 1. Make Your Plan
sections.text: This book has 13 chapters. Plan the whole book before Chapter 1.
points: Choose your study days and how many chapters you will read each week.
Write one personal goal for this book.
Save new words to My words and review them after one day, three days and one week.

sections.title: 2. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 25 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and the “Before You Read” question.
Read for the main idea.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 3. Read and Listen
sections.text: Read every chapter twice: once for the main idea, once for the details. When the audio is ready, listen once while you follow the text.
points: First reading: What is the chapter about?
Second reading: Mark names, dates and linking words.
Say one long sentence aloud with the right pauses.

sections.title: 4. Word Notes
sections.text: Bold words have Word Notes. Use them after you have tried to understand the sentence yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Write the word in a new sentence of your own.

sections.title: 5. Quick Challenge
sections.text: Answer before you read the feedback. If you are wrong, repair the answer with the text.
points: Find the paragraph the question is about.
Read the key sentence again.
Explain why the right answer is right, then try again.

sections.title: 6. Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has 4 Language Focus activities built from the chapter’s own sentences.
points: Activity 1 (Notice): Look at a sentence and what it means.
Activities 2–3 (Build): Choose, complete, correct or rewrite forms.
Activity 4 (Use): Write or say connected sentences about a different situation.

sections.title: 7. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Some chapters have many names and dates. Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Read one paragraph only.
Make a time line of the dates.
List the names and what each one did.
Learn only three words today.

sections.title: 8. Values in the Book
sections.text: The book shows respect, helpfulness, responsibility and diligence. Find the sentence first, then think of a small action of your own.
points: Respect: Respect: Turkic peoples still respect Yesevî, and he asked people not to hurt anyone, even non-believers (Chapters 5, 7 and 13).
Helpfulness: Helpfulness: Yesevî wrote about caring for orphans and strangers and helping oppressed people (Chapter 7).
Responsibility: Responsibility: Teachers must treat their students with love and kindness so that they focus on the lessons (Chapter 8).
Diligence: Diligence: Yesevî studied with great teachers in Yesi and Bukhara, and education and self-discipline are very important on the path of wisdom (Chapters 3 and 7).

sections.title: 9. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 13, do the review pages in this order. Go back to a chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Knowledge Check
Vocabulary Challenge
Master Glossary
Language Review
Final Challenge

sections.title: 10. Look Back
sections.text: Before Chapter 1 and again at the end, answer the “I can” statements of a few chapters. What can you do now that you could not do before?
points: Which chapter changed what you knew?
Tell someone at home in five sentences who Ahmed Yesevî was and why he chose Turkish, in your home language or in English.
